A tourniquet is a device used to stop severe bleeding from a limb — an arm or a leg — by tightly squeezing the limb to cut off blood flow to the wound.

When you have a deep cut or injury on your arm or leg that is bleeding heavily and won't stop, your body is losing blood fast. Blood travels from your heart through blood vessels called arteries and veins that run through your limbs. A tourniquet works by pressing down hard enough on the limb — from the outside — to compress those vessels completely. When the vessels are compressed, blood simply cannot flow through them anymore, so the bleeding stops.

Think of it like pinching a garden hose tightly with your hand. Even though water is flowing through it with pressure, your grip cuts off the flow. A tourniquet does exactly that to your blood vessels — but using a band wrapped around the limb instead of fingers.

A tourniquet is typically a wide, flat band or strap that wraps around the limb, with some mechanism to tighten it further — usually a rotating stick or rod called a windlass, or a tightening buckle. The strap goes around the limb (above the wound, closer to the body), and then you twist or pull it tighter and tighter until the bleeding stops.

In emergencies when no proper tourniquet is available, people have improvised one using a strip of cloth, a belt, or even a shirt — combined with a pen or stick to twist it tighter. These are called improvised tourniquets. However, purpose-made tourniquets (like the CAT — Combat Application Tourniquet) are far more reliable and are standard in military kits, ambulances, and first-aid supplies worldwide.

A tourniquet is used in situations where bleeding is life-threatening and cannot be controlled by simple pressure. This includes:

  • Traumatic injuries — such as a limb being severely cut, crushed, or partially or fully severed (amputated), often in accidents, explosions, or combat.
  • Surgical settings — surgeons sometimes use tourniquets deliberately during operations on limbs to create a bloodless field so they can see clearly and work precisely.
  • Animal bites or deep lacerations that have damaged a major blood vessel.

It is not used for every cut or wound. It is a last resort for serious, uncontrollable bleeding because it comes with real risks (explained below).

The tourniquet is always placed above the wound — meaning between the wound and the heart. This is important because blood flows from the heart outward, so placing it above the wound blocks blood from reaching the wound site in the first place.

For example, if someone has a deep gash on their lower arm, the tourniquet goes on the upper arm — not below the wound. If the injury is on the lower leg, it goes on the upper leg (thigh area).

Once in place, it is tightened until the bleeding visibly stops. The time it was applied is noted (written on the skin or on the device itself), because how long a tourniquet has been on is critical information for doctors.

Severe bleeding from a limb can cause a person to bleed out and die within minutes. The heart keeps pumping blood to that limb, and if a large blood vessel is cut, the blood loss is rapid and catastrophic. A tourniquet, properly applied, can keep someone alive long enough to reach medical care.

This is why tourniquets are carried by soldiers, paramedics, emergency responders, and are increasingly part of public first-aid kits in schools, offices, and event venues. Many lives have been saved in mass casualty events (like bombings or shootings) specifically because bystanders applied tourniquets before paramedics arrived.

A tourniquet is powerful but not without danger. Because it cuts off all blood flow to the limb, the tissues below it start to be deprived of oxygen. If a tourniquet is left on for too long — generally, more than one to two hours without medical intervention — the tissue can begin to die, potentially leading to permanent nerve damage or, in extreme cases, the need to amputate the limb.

This is why tourniquets are considered an emergency bridge measure, not a treatment. The goal is always to get the person to a hospital as fast as possible.

Also, applying a tourniquet too loosely is dangerous — a loose tourniquet can block the veins (which carry blood back to the heart) while still allowing the arteries (which carry blood to the limb) to pump blood in. This actually makes bleeding worse. A proper tourniquet must be tight enough to stop arterial flow entirely.

A tourniquet is a tightly-wrapped band applied around a limb to completely stop blood flow and control life-threatening bleeding. It is a critical emergency tool — simple in concept, life-saving in action, but requiring proper application and time awareness. It buys time. It doesn't heal. Its job is to keep a person alive until real medical treatment is possible.
